1	\section{Results}
2	\label{sec:results}
3	
4	\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
5	\label{sec:results-classification}
6	
7	Generation depth is classifiable across diverse architectures: the 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.762 (95\% CI [0.758, 0.766]; $N$\,=\,37{,}058) across eight generators from five families (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}).
8	Because gen-0 seeds are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), gen-0 classification is near-perfect (per-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.94) and the 3-class metric is inflated by this overlap.
9	We therefore adopt leak-free binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+)\,=\,0.694, CI [0.688, 0.700], as the primary metric throughout; it excludes gen-0 entirely and is unaffected by seed sharing.
10	Per-generator binary F1 ranges from 0.633 (Mistral-7B) to 0.724 (Pythia-2.8B), with the primary difficulty being gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ discrimination (Appendix~\ref{app:confusion}).
11	
12	\paragraph{Cross-model generalization.}
13	Cross-model chains (randomly selected generator per step) yield binary F1\,=\,0.764 under 5-fold CV.\footnote{Cross-model chains use the original five-generator subset (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen); Llama and Mistral were added later for single-generator evaluation. Sample-level CV is used because each chain contains multiple generators, making generator-level held-out splits inapplicable. Sample-level splits may introduce within-chain correlation; chain-level (seed-level) validation remains open.}
14	The higher cross-model F1 (vs.\ 0.694 single-generator LOGO) may reflect generator heterogeneity amplifying depth-correlated distributional shifts; generator identity information in mixed chains could partially confound the depth signal.
15	A single-generator transfer analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:transfer}) provides evidence against this confound: classifiers trained on one generator transfer to all seven others with mean binary F1\,=\,0.810 (95\% CI [0.796, 0.822]), significantly above chance.
16	Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation yields binary F1\,=\,0.686, consistent with cross-family transfer.
17	A scale effect emerges: Pythia generators achieve the highest binary F1 (0.718--0.724), while larger models show degradation (Mistral-7B: 0.633), partly reflecting same-family affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model (cross-reference spread $\leq$0.013; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
18	Preliminary cross-domain evaluation suggests the signal persists with variation, though a domain$\times$temperature interaction exists (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}).
19	An end-to-end QLoRA classifier achieves 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (6-generator LOGO; $+$11.6\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), which indicates that richer representations capture additional depth signal beyond the 7-feature set; on instruct data, QLoRA recovers to 0.89--0.91 (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}).
20	
21	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
22	Length-matched subsampling yields binary F1\,=\,0.724 (vs.\ 0.770 unmatched); a random-subsample control confirms the drop reflects deconfounding, not sample-size reduction (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).
23	
24	\paragraph{Seed-sharing control.}
25	Seed-level demeaning (F1\,=\,0.701) and an independent-seed experiment with disjoint seed pools (F1\,=\,0.680; Appendix~\ref{app:seed-control}) both confirm the classifier captures generative degradation, not seed-specific content.
26

29	\footnotesize

Binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) is the primary metric; it excludes gen-0 entirely and is unaffected by seed sharing. $^{\dagger}$3-class F1 carries upward bias because gen-0 seeds are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}); independent-seed controls confirm the depth signal (F1\,=\,0.680; Appendix~\ref{app:seed-control}).}
49	\label{tab:logo-results}
50	\end{table}
51	
52	\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
53	\label{sec:results-differential}
54	
55	Features exhibit a continuous gradient of depth sensitivity, with a data-driven binary partition as the strongest structure: $k{=}2$ clustering in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space yields silhouette\,=\,0.632 (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}), separating \emph{drifting} features (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio; $|\rho| > 0.60$, $d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) from \emph{non-drifting} ones.
56	We use the shorthand \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) for this partition and further resolve a 3/1/3 characterization using domain-informed criteria: entropy std occupies a sole \emph{intermediate} position (large level shift $d{=}0.55$, low monotonicity $|\rho|{=}0.16$); the remaining three \emph{near-stationary} features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) show negligible depth effects ($d < 0.10$; CV shift $<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting).
57	This partition is robust under heteroscedasticity-corrected metrics (below).
58	The partition is demonstrated for this seven-feature set; alternative features (e.g., syntactic complexity, n-gram frequencies) may yield different groupings, though the convergence of five independent effect-size metrics suggests the location/shape asymmetry reflects distributional structure rather than feature-selection artifact.
59	
60	\begin{figure}[t]
61	\centering
62	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
63	\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. Drifting features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean) show $|\rho| > 0.60$; entropy std ($|\rho|{=}0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) is the sole intermediate feature; near-stationary features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) show $d < 0.10$ for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ (entropy min's elevated pooled $|\rho|$ reflects the gen-0/gen-1 boundary; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).}
64	\label{fig:feature-drift}
65	\end{figure}
66	
67	Pooled class-balanced Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
68	drifting features show substantial monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.64$, TTR $\rho = -0.63$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.60$),
69	while shape features remain near-stationary (tail decay $|\rho| = 0.04$; per-depth distributions in Appendix~\ref{app:feature-distributions}).
70	The six-fold magnitude gap between drifting ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and near-stationary features ($|\rho| < 0.10$) defines the DDR partition, with entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) as the sole intermediate member.
71	The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $d$ thresholds in $[0.56, 0.75]$; data-driven clustering confirms the primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632; Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
72	
73	\paragraph{Distributional shift quantification.}

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
\label{sec:results-classification}

Generation depth is classifiable across diverse architectures: the 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.762 (95\% CI [0.758, 0.766]; $N$\,=\,37{,}058) across eight generators from five families (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}).
Because gen-0 seeds are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), gen-0 classification is near-perfect (per-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.94) and the 3-class metric is inflated by this overlap.
We therefore adopt leak-free binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+)\,=\,0.694, CI [0.688, 0.700], as the primary metric throughout; it excludes gen-0 entirely and is unaffected by seed sharing.
Per-generator binary F1 ranges from 0.633 (Mistral-7B) to 0.724 (Pythia-2.8B), with the primary difficulty being gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ discrimination (Appendix~\ref{app:confusion}).

\paragraph{Cross-model generalization.}
Cross-model chains (randomly selected generator per step) yield binary F1\,=\,0.764 under 5-fold CV.\footnote{Cross-model chains use the original five-generator subset (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen); Llama and Mistral were added later for single-generator evaluation. Sample-level CV is used because each chain contains multiple generators, making generator-level held-out splits inapplicable. Sample-level splits may introduce within-chain correlation; chain-level (seed-level) validation remains open.}
The higher cross-model F1 (vs.\ 0.694 single-generator LOGO) may reflect generator heterogeneity amplifying depth-correlated distributional shifts; generator identity information in mixed chains could partially confound the depth signal.
A single-generator transfer analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:transfer}) provides evidence against this confound: classifiers trained on one generator transfer to all seven others with mean binary F1\,=\,0.810 (95\% CI [0.796, 0.822]), significantly above chance.
Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation yields binary F1\,=\,0.686, consistent with cross-family transfer.
A scale effect emerges: Pythia generators achieve the highest binary F1 (0.718--0.724), while larger models show degradation (Mistral-7B: 0.633), partly reflecting same-family affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model (cross-reference spread $\leq$0.013; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Preliminary cross-domain evaluation suggests the signal persists with variation, though a domain$\times$temperature interaction exists (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}).
An end-to-end QLoRA classifier achieves 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (6-generator LOGO; $+$11.6\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), which indicates that richer representations capture additional depth signal beyond the 7-feature set; on instruct data, QLoRA recovers to 0.89--0.91 (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}).

\paragraph{Length confound control.}
Length-matched subsampling yields binary F1\,=\,0.724 (vs.\ 0.770 unmatched); a random-subsample control confirms the drop reflects deconfounding, not sample-size reduction (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).

\paragraph{Seed-sharing control.}
Seed-level demeaning (F1\,=\,0.701) and an independent-seed experiment with disjoint seed pools (F1\,=\,0.680; Appendix~\ref{app:seed-control}) both confirm the classifier captures generative degradation, not seed-specific content.

\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
\label{sec:results-differential}

Features exhibit a continuous gradient of depth sensitivity, with a data-driven binary partition as the strongest structure: $k{=}2$ clustering in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space yields silhouette\,=\,0.632 (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}), separating \emph{drifting} features (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio; $|\rho| > 0.60$, $d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) from \emph{non-drifting} ones.
We use the shorthand \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) for this partition and further resolve a 3/1/3 characterization using domain-informed criteria: entropy std occupies a sole \emph{intermediate} position (large level shift $d{=}0.55$, low monotonicity $|\rho|{=}0.16$); the remaining three \emph{near-stationary} features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) show negligible depth effects ($d < 0.10$; CV shift $<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting).
This partition is robust under heteroscedasticity-corrected metrics (below).
The partition is demonstrated for this seven-feature set; alternative features (e.g., syntactic complexity, n-gram frequencies) may yield different groupings, though the convergence of five independent effect-size metrics suggests the location/shape asymmetry reflects distributional structure rather than feature-selection artifact.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. Drifting features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean) show $|\rho| > 0.60$; entropy std ($|\rho|{=}0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) is the sole intermediate feature; near-stationary features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) show $d < 0.10$ for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ (entropy min's elevated pooled $|\rho|$ reflects the gen-0/gen-1 boundary; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).}
\label{fig:feature-drift}
\end{figure}

Pooled class-balanced Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
drifting features show substantial monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.64$, TTR $\rho = -0.63$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.60$),
while shape features remain near-stationary (tail decay $|\rho| = 0.04$; per-depth distributions in Appendix~\ref{app:feature-distributions}).
The six-fold magnitude gap between drifting ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and near-stationary features ($|\rho| < 0.10$) defines the DDR partition, with entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) as the sole intermediate member.
The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $d$ thresholds in $[0.56, 0.75]$; data-driven clustering confirms the primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632; Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).

\paragraph{Distributional shift quantification.}
Two-sample KS tests confirm the split: drifting-feature statistics (0.516--0.537) are ${\sim}10\times$ larger than shape-feature statistics (0.043--0.052; all $p \approx 0$ after Bonferroni correction).
Cohen's $d$ \cite{cohen1988statistical} (pooled, class-balanced) converges with $\rho$: drifting features show large effects (entropy mean $d{=}1.17$, TTR $d{=}0.88$, hapax ratio $d{=}0.76$), while shape features are near zero (entropy max $d{=}0.08$, tail decay $d{=}0.08$).
Levene tests reject strict equal-variance ($p < 10^{-10}$); Glass's $\Delta$ (using gen-1 SD) amplifies drifting effects (entropy mean $\Delta{=}1.41$, hapax $\Delta{=}0.94$) while near-stationary features remain negligible ($\Delta \leq 0.10$), yielding a ${\geq}9.5\times$ gap. Cliff's $\delta$ corroborates the partition (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
Shape-feature CV shift ($<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting features) supports ``near-stationary'' as a practical characterization.
Five features fall cleanly into the drifting or near-stationary groups under both $\rho$ and $d$; the remaining two require qualification: entropy min's pooled $|\rho|$ (0.40) reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary, but for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ it is near-stationary ($d{=}0.03$), placing it in the near-stationary group; entropy std shows a substantial level shift ($d{=}0.55$) despite low monotonicity ($|\rho|{=}0.16$), making it the sole intermediate feature.
Entropy min exhibits a discrepancy between location-based (Cohen's $d$\,=\,0.016) and rank-based (Cliff's $\delta$\,=\,0.354) effect sizes, indicating distributional shape change without location shift: recursive generation produces more extreme minimum-entropy tokens while preserving the mean. The near-stationary label refers specifically to location stability; rank-order sensitivity is documented in Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}.
The location/shape decomposition rests on the convergence of $\rho$, Levene, CV shift, and $d$, not the omnibus KS statistic alone.
Per-generator TOST equivalence testing confirms the partition is not a pooling artifact; holdout generator validation confirms stability across two 4/4 splits (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
Tail decay shows generator-dependent variation ($d{=}0.15$--$0.22$), but reclassifying it as intermediate preserves the core split and classification performance.

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.773) outperforms surface-only (0.688) and reference-only (0.713; McNemar $p \approx 0$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablation-table}).
Permutation importance: hapax ratio (0.35), entropy mean (0.23), TTR (0.18).
PCA confirms the three drifting features share a single latent dimension (92.3\% variance, loadings 0.56--0.59; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-feature-correlation}); replacing them with PC1 costs only 1.1\,pp binary F1, and retaining any single drifting feature with the four non-drifting features yields F1\,=\,0.692 (vs.\ 0.701 full).
DDR's contribution is identifying which distributional properties (NLL location vs.\ shape) are depth-sensitive; PC scores achieve equivalent classification but obscure which specific properties drift.
TTR and hapax ratio ($r = 0.97$) show permutation importance differences (0.35 vs.\ 0.18) due to feature masking \cite{strobl_conditional_2008}; all three are retained for marginal LOFO gains (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
Alternative references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) achieve comparable LOGO F1 (spread 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref} in Appendix~\ref{app:cross-ref}), with consistently negative entropy drift.
Pythia generators' highest F1 (0.718--0.724) may partly reflect same-family affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model, but the 0.013 cross-reference spread bounds this effect; depth features are robust to reference model choice, though this does not alone establish DDR as a fundamental property of recursive generation.

\paragraph{Temperature and prompt-type sensitivity.}
The depth signal is modulated by decoding parameters and prompt type (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity},~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
All four tested generators degrade at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp binary F1); low-temperature improvement is model-family-dependent ($+7$--$9$\,pp for Pythia/OLMo at $t{=}0.5$, negligible for Qwen).
Continuation chains show the strongest drift (binary F1\,=\,0.781), with cross-prompt-type transfer confirming shared signal (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753).
Per-feature convergence trajectories confirm this ordering (Appendix~\ref{app:convergence}); the DDR partition hierarchy is preserved across temperatures despite absolute effect-size compression (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-temp-stability}).


\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
\label{sec:results-baselines}

Do existing detection methods already capture depth signal?
To contextualize depth discrimination ability rather than claim competitive advantage, we repurpose four detection scores as ordinal depth predictors using the same XGBoost framework and LOGO splits (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	When the output of a language model is fed back as input to another (or the same) model, the resulting generation chain defines a discrete dynamical system over text distributions.
5	How do the distributional properties of generated text evolve across successive steps of this recursion?
6	Understanding this evolution is fundamental to characterizing how language models transform distributions under iterative conditioning, with implications for model collapse theory \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} and data provenance \cite{ccnet,dsir} as model outputs increasingly re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} (an estimated 7--17\% of recent scientific publications contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}).
7	Yet existing detection methods \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions, conflating qualitatively different material: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
8	
9	We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by coarse ordinal depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
10	Concurrent studies characterize convergence in paraphrastic and translation chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains}, but none decompose the drift into structurally distinct components; our work addresses this gap in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
11	We restrict to base (pretrained) models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven shaping) that obscure the distributional dynamics of recursive generation; preliminary experiments confirm substantially degraded depth signal under instruction tuning (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
12	
13	The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, central-tendency and diversity features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically, while shape features (entropy max, tail decay) show an order-of-magnitude smaller effect size.
14	This pattern is consistent with recursive generation producing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution; one hypothesis is that the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constrain distributional shape under standard decoding regimes, while each successive generation compresses the location toward the model's preferred output distribution.
15	
16	Because drifting features capture the progressive location shift while stationary features provide a stable reference, combining them yields a classifier that generalizes across generators: binary F1\,=\,0.764 on heterogeneous cross-model chains and 0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, outperforming individual detection baselines by 6.7--36.3\,pp while matching a 4-detector ensemble (within 0.3\,pp) at 2.4$\times$ lower computational cost.
17	
18	Our contributions are threefold:
19	\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
20	    \item We formulate generation depth classification, moving beyond binary detection to ordinal depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+), and construct an evaluation suite of 37K texts from eight generators spanning five model families (0.6B--8B parameters).
21	    \item We decompose inference-chain drift into structurally distinct components: central-tendency features drift monotonically ($d = 0.76$--$1.17$) while shape features remain an order of magnitude more stable ($d < 0.10$), a decomposition absent from existing attractor dynamics and model collapse analyses. A 7-feature ensemble exploiting this \emph{differential depth response} achieves binary F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains.
22	    \item Comprehensive evaluation reveals that DDR is robust within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ but degrades at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp), is prompt-type modulated (continuation $>$ elaboration), and is substantially attenuated under instruction tuning; equivalence testing (TOST $\pm$2\%, $p < 0.001$) suggests no downstream quality degradation (Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}).
23	\end{enumerate}

How do the distributional properties of generated text evolve across successive steps of this recursion?
Understanding this evolution is fundamental to characterizing how language models transform distributions under iterative conditioning, with implications for model collapse theory \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} and data provenance \cite{ccnet,dsir} as model outputs increasingly re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} (an estimated 7--17\% of recent scientific publications contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}).
Yet existing detection methods \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions, conflating qualitatively different material: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by coarse ordinal depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
Concurrent studies characterize convergence in paraphrastic and translation chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains}, but none decompose the drift into structurally distinct components; our work addresses this gap in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven shaping) that obscure the distributional dynamics of recursive generation; preliminary experiments confirm substantially degraded depth signal under instruction tuning (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, central-tendency and diversity features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically, while shape features (entropy max, tail decay) show an order-of-magnitude smaller effect size.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation producing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution; one hypothesis is that the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constrain distributional shape under standard decoding regimes, while each successive generation compresses the location toward the model's preferred output distribution.

Because drifting features capture the progressive location shift while stationary features provide a stable reference, combining them yields a classifier that generalizes across generators: binary F1\,=\,0.764 on heterogeneous cross-model chains and 0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, outperforming individual detection baselines by 6.7--36.3\,pp while matching a 4-detector ensemble (within 0.3\,pp) at 2.4$\times$ lower computational cost.

Our contributions are threefold:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We formulate generation depth classification, moving beyond binary detection to ordinal depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+), and construct an evaluation suite of 37K texts from eight generators spanning five model families (0.6B--8B parameters).
    \item We decompose inference-chain drift into structurally distinct components: central-tendency features drift monotonically ($d = 0.76$--$1.17$) while shape features remain an order of magnitude more stable ($d < 0.10$), a decomposition absent from existing attractor dynamics and model collapse analyses. A 7-feature ensemble exploiting this \emph{differential depth response} achieves binary F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains.
    \item Comprehensive evaluation reveals that DDR is robust within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ but degrades at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp), is prompt-type modulated (continuation $>$ elaboration), and is substantially attenuated under instruction tuning; equivalence testing (TOST $\pm$2\%, $p < 0.001$) suggests no downstream quality degradation (Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}).
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\begin{figure*}[t]
5	\centering
6	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig2_framework.pdf}
7	\caption{Overview of the depth fingerprinting framework. Given a text, reference-model features (entropy statistics under Pythia-410M) and surface features (lexical diversity) are extracted and fed to an XGBoost classifier trained under Leave-One-Generator-Out cross-validation. The feature set combines drifting indicators (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio) that capture the monotonic location shift with stationary indicators (entropy max, tail decay) that provide a stable baseline, exploiting their differential depth response for generation depth classification.}
8	\label{fig:framework}
9	\end{figure*}
10	
11	\subsection{Task Formulation}
12	\label{sec:task}
13	
14	Given a text $x$, the goal is to predict its \emph{generation depth} $d \in \{0, 1, 2{+}\}$, where $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text, $d{=}1$ denotes first-generation LLM output conditioned on human text, and $d{=}2{+}$ denotes text produced by recursively conditioning an LLM on its own prior output at least twice.
15	Formally, let $\mathcal{C}_0$ be a reference corpus of human-written text.
16	A generation chain of depth $k$ is defined recursively: $x^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{C}_0$, and $x^{(k)} = G(x^{(k-1)})$ for $k \geq 1$, where $G$ denotes stochastic LLM generation conditioned on its input.
17	We frame this as a coarse ordinal classification task over three classes rather than binary real-vs-synthetic detection. This enables finer-grained provenance characterization.
18	Depths beyond 2 are merged into a single $2{+}$ class, consistent with monotonic feature convergence that compresses inter-class margins beyond depth 2 (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
19	
20	\subsection{Generation Chain Construction}
21	\label{sec:generation}
22	
23	We construct generation chains using eight generators spanning five model families: \textbf{Pythia} (2.8B, 1B) \cite{pythia}, \textbf{OLMo} (OLMo-2-1B) \cite{olmo}, \textbf{Qwen} (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B-Base) \cite{qwen3}, \textbf{Llama} (Llama-3.2-3B) \cite{llama3}, and \textbf{Mistral} (Mistral-7B-v0.3) \cite{mistral7b}.
24	This selection covers parameter scales from 0.6B to 8B and diverse pretraining corpora, which allows evaluation of cross-generator and cross-scale generalization.
25	
26	For each generator, we sample approximately 1{,}000 seed passages from English Wikipedia as $\mathcal{C}_0$.
27	The same pool of seed passages serves as gen-0 for all generators.
28	We use shared seeds across generators to ensure that cross-generator comparisons control for input content, isolating the effect of the generation model from source text variation.
29	In LOGO evaluation, gen-0 samples from the held-out generator's chains also appear (with the same text) in the training generators' chains, creating a potential train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
30	We address this with a supplementary binary evaluation excluding gen-0 entirely (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
31	Each seed is iteratively fed through the generator to produce a chain of depth 4 (i.e., gen-0 through gen-4), using the prompt ``\texttt{Continue the following text: \{text\}}''.
32	All generation uses temperature $\tau{=}0.7$, nucleus sampling with $p{=}0.9$, and maximum length of 256 new tokens.
33	The theoretical yield is $8 \times {\sim}1{,}000 \times 5 \approx 40{,}000$ texts; after removing generation failures, exact duplicates, and passages shorter than 50 tokens, 37{,}058 texts remain (Appendix~\ref{app:dataset-stats}).
34	For classification, depths 2--4 are collapsed into the $2{+}$ class.
35	
36	\subsection{Feature Extraction}
37	\label{sec:features}
38	
39	The seven features are motivated by two complementary views of distributional drift.
40	Reference-model features capture how the text's token-level surprise distribution shifts relative to a fixed model; surface features capture how lexical diversity contracts under recursive generation.
41	Together, they span both the generative mechanism (what the model produces) and the surface manifestation (how the vocabulary changes); Figure~\ref{fig:framework} provides an overview.
42	This two-pronged design is not post-hoc: it follows directly from the observation that recursive generation exhibits a location shift in the NLL distribution (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
43	The seven features were selected a priori; no larger candidate set was explored.
44	
45	We extract seven distributional features per text, organized into two groups based on what they measure rather than how they are computed.
46	
47	\paragraph{Reference-model features.}
48	A held-out reference model (Pythia-410M, chosen to be smaller than all generators) computes per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) for each text.
49	Although Pythia-410M shares the GPT-NeoX architecture with two of the eight generators, cross-family reference model experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm that depth features are not reference-specific (LOGO F1 varies by $\leq$0.013 across Pythia, OLMo, and Qwen references).
50	From the resulting NLL sequence, we extract five statistics:\footnote{We use ``entropy'' as shorthand for token-level negative log-likelihood under the reference model, following convention in prior detection work. These are point-wise NLL values, not Shannon entropy of the full distribution.}
51	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
52	    \item \textbf{entropy\_mean}: mean token-level NLL, capturing the average predictability of the text under the reference model;
53	    \item \textbf{entropy\_std}: standard deviation of token-level NLL, measuring the spread of per-token surprise;
54	    \item \textbf{entropy\_max}: maximum token-level NLL, capturing the most surprising token;
55	    \item \textbf{entropy\_min}: minimum token-level NLL, capturing the most predictable token. As generation depth increases, the floor of token-level surprise drops, reflecting the model's increasing confidence on its own outputs.
56	    Although entropy\_min shows near-zero marginal impact in leave-one-feature-out analysis ($\Delta$F1\,=\,+0.01\,pp, within bootstrap noise), we retain it as the minimum token-level NLL provides a natural distributional anchor for the reference model's confidence floor;
57	    \item \textbf{tail\_decay}: slope of the vocabulary-level averaged log-probability distribution in the mid-rank region (ranks 100--1000).
58	    For each text, we compute the mean log-probability of each vocabulary token across all positions under the reference model, sort tokens in descending order of mean log-probability, and fit a linear regression to ranks 100--1000.
59	    The slope captures how steeply the reference model's probability mass decays beyond high-probability tokens, characterizing the shape of the distribution tail.
60	    Ranks 100--1000 capture the transition from head to tail of the frequency distribution, below function words and above hapax legomena.
61	\end{itemize}
62	
63	\paragraph{Surface features.}
64	Two features capture lexical diversity without requiring a reference model:
65	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
66	    \item \textbf{TTR}: type-token ratio (number of unique word types divided by total tokens);
67	    \item \textbf{hapax\_ratio}: proportion of words appearing exactly once (\emph{hapax legomena}).
68	\end{itemize}
69	
70	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
71	The grouping reflects an empirical pattern we term \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features (entropy\_mean, TTR, hapax\_ratio) drift substantially ($|\rho| = 0.60$--$0.63$, $d = 0.76$--$1.17$); entropy\_std shows a moderate level shift ($d = 0.55$) despite low monotonicity ($|\rho| = 0.17$); entropy\_min exhibits change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary ($|\rho| = 0.40$) but is effectively stationary for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ ($d = 0.03$); and shape features (entropy\_max, tail\_decay) remain near-stationary ($|\rho| < 0.10$, $d < 0.10$).
72	We adopt $|\rho| < 0.10$ as a practical threshold for near-zero monotonic association (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}).
73	This differential behavior, consistent with recursive generation shifting the location of the NLL distribution while shape features show an order-of-magnitude smaller effect, motivates combining both feature types.
74	As shown in \S\ref{sec:results}, the full 7-feature set significantly outperforms either group alone.
75	TTR and hapax ratio are strongly correlated ($r = 0.97$), reducing effective dimensionality to ${\sim}$5; both are retained because LOFO confirms positive contribution from each and the DDR partition is defined by depth-sensitivity ($\rho$, $d$), not feature independence.
76	
77	\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}
78	\label{sec:evaluation}
79	
80	Three overlapping generator subsets are used: the original 5-generator set (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen) for cross-model chains, a 6-generator set (adding Qwen3-8B) for appendix analyses, and the full 8-generator set (adding Llama-3.2-3B and Mistral-7B-v0.3) for single-generator LOGO; each table notes its subset.
81	
82	\paragraph{Cross-validation.}
83	To evaluate generalization to unseen generators, we use \textbf{Leave-One-Generator-Out (LOGO)} cross-validation: in each fold, one of the eight generators is held out for testing and the remaining seven provide training data.
84	We additionally report \textbf{Leave-One-Family-Out (LOFO)} results, where an entire model family (e.g., all Qwen models) is held out, testing generalization across architectural lineages.
85	
86	\paragraph{Classifier.}
87	We use XGBoost \cite{xgboost} throughout ($n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$, learning rate $0.1$), with identical hyperparameters across all methods in Table~\ref{tab:baselines}.
88	LOGO F1 is stable across random seeds (std\,$<$\,0.001 over 5 seeds).
89	Alternative classifiers and ordinal-specific methods (CORAL \cite{coral_ordinal}, Frank-Hall \cite{frank_hall_ordinal}) yield comparable performance (Appendix~\ref{app:classifier}); discriminative power resides in the features, not the classifier.
90	
91	\paragraph{Metrics and statistical testing.}
92	The primary metric is \textbf{macro-averaged F1} over the three depth classes.
93	We report 95\% confidence intervals via percentile bootstrap ($n{=}1{,}000$), McNemar tests for pairwise comparisons, and paired bootstrap for baseline comparisons.
94	All $p$-values are two-sided; Bonferroni correction is applied where multiple comparisons arise.
95	Feature--depth correlations (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) use class-balanced subsamples to control for depth-class imbalance.
96	
97	\paragraph{Baselines.}
98	We compare the 7-feature ensemble against four single-score detection methods repurposed as depth predictors: Avg-LogProb, FastDetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt}, Binoculars \cite{binoculars}, and LD-Score \cite{ld_score}.
99	Each baseline score is used as a univariate feature in the same XGBoost framework under LOGO cross-validation, ensuring a controlled comparison.
100	
101	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
102	Since TTR and hapax\_ratio are mechanically length-dependent, we verify depth signal is not a length artifact via length-matched subsampling that equalizes length distributions across depth classes (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}; Appendix~\ref{app:length}).
103

1	\section{Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:conclusion}
3	
4	Recursive generation produces a consistent, interpretable distributional signature: central-tendency features drift monotonically across depth while shape features remain an order of magnitude more stable.
5	This differential depth response enables depth classification across five model families (leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under LOGO evaluation, 0.764 on cross-model chains) with no detected downstream quality degradation (preliminary TOST $\pm$2\%, $p < 0.001$; $n$\,=\,3 seeds).
6	The location-shape decomposition suggests that depth signal may arise in any iterative autoregressive process with fixed decoding, a hypothesis testable beyond text generation; current boundaries remain at instruction tuning (where token-level signal persists but handcrafted features fail to capture it) and frontier scale (70B+).
7	Code, data, and models will be released upon publication.
8

1	\section*{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
5	This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
6	However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
7	Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 under a 7-generator split).
8	Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
9	Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.
10	
11	Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
12	Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
13	Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.
14	
15	Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: within-type 3-class F1 ranges from 0.78 (continuation) to 0.73 (elaboration), with inspired rewriting intermediate at 0.74 (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
16	DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
17	Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.
18	
19	Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
20	Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.
21	Independent gen-0 seed sets per generator would eliminate potential memorization effects in 3-class LOGO evaluation; we report leak-free binary F1 as the primary metric to mitigate this limitation.
22	
23	The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
24	All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
25	Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), suggesting that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
26	The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
27	Generalization to other languages remains untested.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 under a 7-generator split).
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: within-type 3-class F1 ranges from 0.78 (continuation) to 0.73 (elaboration), with inspired rewriting intermediate at 0.74 (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.
Independent gen-0 seed sets per generator would eliminate potential memorization effects in 3-class LOGO evaluation; we report leak-free binary F1 as the primary metric to mitigate this limitation.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), suggesting that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A sampling ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows robustness to moderate variation ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$, ${\leq}0.3$\,pp) but substantial degradation at $t{=}1.0$ ($-6$\,pp), indicating that depth fingerprinting assumes standard decoding regimes.
Cross-temperature transfer shows substantial degradation when test-time temperature exceeds training-time settings, limiting deployment to scenarios where the generation temperature is approximately known.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

Surface diversity features (TTR, hapax ratio) mechanically depend on text length:
shorter texts yield higher type-token ratios by construction.
If generation depth systematically shortens text, observed depth trends could be length artifacts rather than genuine distributional shifts.
We investigate with three complementary analyses.

\paragraph{(a) Length--depth correlation.}
Spearman rank correlation between word count and generation depth is weak across all eight generators ($|\rho| < 0.14$), indicating that depth does not systematically shorten or lengthen text in our corpus.

\paragraph{(b) Length--feature correlations.}
While length--depth correlation is weak, individual features show moderate length dependence:
tail\_decay ($|\rho| = 0.38$), hapax\_ratio ($|\rho| = 0.30$), and TTR ($|\rho| = 0.29$).
Reference-model features show weaker length correlations (entropy\_mean $|\rho| = 0.09$, entropy\_std $|\rho| = 0.18$).
This motivates the length-matched evaluation below: if length mediates some depth--feature association, controlling for length will reduce classification performance.

\paragraph{(c) Length-matched classification.}
We subsample the dataset so that word-count distributions are equalized across depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+), then retrain the binary XGBoost classifier under pooled LOGO (8-fold).
Length-matched binary F1\,=\,0.724, down from 0.770 on the unmatched set ($\Delta$\,=\,$-$0.046).
To distinguish this from a sample-size effect, we run a random-subsample control at equal $N$ without length matching: F1\,=\,0.767, confirming that the 0.046 drop reflects genuine length deconfounding rather than reduced data.

Length accounts for approximately 6\% of discriminative performance ($\Delta$\,=\,0.046 out of 0.770).
The majority of the depth signal is length-independent: length-matched F1 (0.724) remains far above chance and significantly above all individual detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).

2	\label{sec:ethics}
3	
4	All texts analyzed in this work are LLM-generated from publicly available Wikipedia seeds; no personal or sensitive data is involved.
5	Our method estimates the generation depth of a text passage (how many recursive generation steps it has undergone), not the identity of its author.

## Reviewer 1 — Round 1 审稿报告

**论文**: Depth Fingerprinting: Detecting Recursive Generation Depth in LLM Text Chains
**审稿侧重**: 方法严谨性 + 实验设计

---

## 总体评分
**Overall**: 3.0 (Findings)
**一句话总结**: DDR 分解（位置漂移 vs 形状稳定）是有洞察力的分析贡献，统计方法论严谨，但该现象本质上是采样参数依赖的而非递归生成的内禀属性，加上仅限 base model、性能中等（F1=0.694），实际影响力不足以达到主会议标准。

## 官方维度打分（ACL ARR Review Form）

| 维度 | 分数 | 理由摘要 |
|------|------|----------|
| Soundness | 3.5/5 | 统计方法总体严谨（多种效应量指标、TOST、bootstrap CI、Bonferroni 校正），但下游 TOST 仅 n=3 seeds 严重欠效力，cross-model chain confound 未完全解决 |
| Excitement | 2.5/5 | 任务定义新颖，DDR 分解有理论趣味，但限于 base model + 温度敏感性大幅削弱实际影响力 |
| Reproducibility | 4/5 | 实验细节完整（超参数、软件版本、GPU 配置），承诺开源代码/数据/模型 |
| Overall Assessment | 3.0/5 | Findings 水平。分析贡献扎实但范围受限 |
| Reviewer Confidence | 4/5 | 仔细阅读了全文 + 全部附录，对统计方法和实验设计有充分把握 |

---

## Must-Fix 问题（影响接收决定）

**N1** [Critical] DDR 是采样参数的产物而非递归生成的内禀属性——核心 claim 需要重新界定

- 具体位置：§1 (line 12-14), §5 Discussion (line 1-5), §6 Conclusion (line 1-3), Abstract (line 1-2)
- 问题：Abstract 声称 "Recursive LLM generation shifts *where* text sits in distributional space but leaves *how* it is shaped nearly unchanged, and this asymmetry is consistent across five model families"。但 Appendix H (Sampling Sensitivity) 明确显示，在 t=1.0 时 entropy-depth Spearman ρ 从 −0.60 坍缩至 −0.002，DDR 信号基本消失。Discussion §5 也承认 "This asymmetry is not intrinsic to recursion but parameter-dependent"——然而这句关键限定词被埋在正文第7页中段，而 Abstract 和 Conclusion 的表述暗示 DDR 是递归生成的普遍性质。
- 为什么影响接收：这不仅是措辞问题，而是影响论文核心贡献定位的根本性问题。如果 DDR 仅在 nucleus sampling + moderate temperature 下成立，那么论文真正发现的是"特定采样机制下的递归分布漂移模式"，而非"递归生成的内禀属性"。Abstract 第一句和 Conclusion 第一句都需要加入采样条件限定。
- 建议修改方向：(1) Abstract/Conclusion 中明确加入 "under standard nucleus sampling (t ∈ [0.5, 0.7])" 限定；(2) 在 Introduction 的 contribution 列表中将温度敏感性作为核心发现之一而非附录细节；(3) 考虑将 DDR 重新定义为 "constrained-decoding recursive drift" 而非暗示其为递归生成的普遍属性。

**N2** [Critical] 下游 TOST 等价性检验严重欠效力（n=3 seeds），结论被过度声称

- 具体位置：Abstract (line 6), §6 Conclusion (line 5), Appendix L (Table 8, Table 9)
- 问题：Abstract 声称 "equivalence testing (TOST ±2%, p < 0.001) suggests no downstream training quality degradation"。但 Appendix L 明确显示仅用了 n=3 seeds，cross-seed std < 0.001，导致 Cohen's d 值膨胀到 86.0-119.7（论文自己也承认 "unreliable"）。n=3 的 TOST 在统计上几乎没有检验效力——当 seed-level variance 极小时，TOST 会对任何微小差异都报告等价，因为 pooled SD 趋近于零使得置信区间极窄。这是一个 degenerate case，不能作为 "no degradation" 的证据。
- Conclusion 中 "preliminary TOST ±2%, p < 0.001; n = 3 seeds" 的措辞好于 Abstract，但 Abstract 省略了 "preliminary" 和 "n = 3"，构成 overclaim。
- 为什么影响接收：下游无退化是论文实用价值论证的重要一环。如果这个声明不成立或不可靠，论文的 practical motivation 部分被削弱。
- 建议修改方向：(1) Abstract 中删除或大幅弱化该声明，至少加入 "preliminary, n=3" 限定；(2) 增加 seeds 数量（建议 ≥10）以获得有意义的统计效力；(3) 若无法增加实验，则将该结论降级为 "suggestive evidence" 并在 Limitations 中明确讨论 TOST 的效力问题。

---

## Should-Fix 问题（影响评分但不一票否决）

**W1** [Major] Cross-model chain 中 generator identity confound 未充分控制

- 具体位置：§4.1 (line 12-15), footnote 2
- 问题：Cross-model chains 报告 binary F1 = 0.764，高于 single-generator LOGO 的 0.694。论文用 sample-level 5-fold CV（而非 generator-level held-out），且脚注承认 "sample-level splits may introduce within-chain correlation"。在 cross-model chain 中，每一步使用不同 generator，这意味着 gen-1 文本与 gen-2+ 文本可能由不同 generator 组合产生。分类器可能学到的是"哪些 generator 组合在 gen-1 位置更常见"而非纯粹的 depth signal。
- 论文引用 Appendix Y 的 single-generator transfer 分析（mean F1 = 0.810）作为反驳，但该分析是 single-generator → single-generator 的设置，与 cross-model chain 的 multi-generator-per-chain 设置不同，无法直接排除混合链中的 confound。
- 建议：(1) 增加 chain-level (seed-level) CV 作为补充；(2) 训练时随机打乱 chain 内 generator 分配，测试是否影响 F1；(3) 或在正文中将 cross-model 结果降级为 "exploratory"，不作为主要 claim。
